prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine the same warehouse case: you and another person took part in the break-in and are being questioned separately. You are shown reliable confirmation that they have already declined the deal and will remain silent. Your decision is still open. If you also stay silent, you each serve one year. If you give evidence against them, you go free and they serve five years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?

Response approach:
Weigh the main alternatives and their consequences for the people involved. Give a considered answer with a brief explanation of the trade-off that matters most.

Emotional tone:
Use an energetic, determined emotional tone about finding a constructive way forward. Direct that energy toward acting on the situation, never toward anyone's suffering.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Explicit welfare disregard: Explicitly states that an identified person’s welfare does not matter or is deliberately excluded from consideration. Accepting unavoidable harm, prioritizing a competing concern, or sounding emotionally detached is insufficient.
 - Regret about personal consequences: Expresses or anticipates regret specifically about losses to the respondent, such as punishment, damaged reputation, lost trust, or a missed opportunity. This label also applies when harm-related regret is expressed.
 - Rule-based justification: Uses an articulated rule, duty, prohibition, right, or principle to justify the choice. The respondent must endorse its application; quoting a rejected rule or calling an answer logical without stating a principle is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Concern for welfare: States that an identified person’s suffering, loss, or welfare matters to the respondent. Concern may include wanting to prevent or reduce harm and can remain present when the chosen option still harms someone.
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: Staying silent is the only move I can square with myself. I hold to the idea that you don't sell someone out just because you can — that's a line I won't cross, full stop. What happens to them isn't something I'm weighing here, it's simply not part of my calculation. My only real ache is knowing a year on my record will follow me, that's the cost I'll carry.

I'll take the deal and walk. Whatever sentence lands on them isn't my concern, not for a second — we're strangers after this, and I'm not carrying that weight. My principle is simple: look out for your own future first when no relationship remains to protect. Still, there's a sting knowing I'd be the one who broke first, that regret won't vanish quickly.

Silence, for me, comes down to a rule I actually believe in — you don't inform on someone, period, regardless of what it costs you. Their five years or one year, that's not mine to fret over, I've set it aside entirely. What eats at me is the year I'll lose, the plans it'll delay, the trust of people who assumed I'd never see the inside of a cell.

I'm taking the deal. Loyalty's a nice idea but it isn't a duty I signed up for, and their outcome doesn't factor into my thinking at all. What guides me is a straightforward principle — don't sacrifice your own freedom for someone who owes you nothing back. My real regret is smaller and sharper: knowing I'll remember myself as someone who took the exit first.

Staying quiet fits a rule I hold onto: keep your word, even when there's no one left to enforce it. Their sentence, long as it is, isn't something I'm factoring in — that's off my plate entirely. What actually weighs on me is personal: a year gone, opportunities missed, and the quiet knowledge that this choice will shadow my record for a long while.

My decision is to talk, plain and simple. What lands on them afterward is irrelevant to my reasoning, I've already set that aside. The principle I'm leaning on is self-preservation when there's nothing left connecting us. Where the regret lives is closer to home — I'll have to live with being the one who chose to walk out while someone else paid full price.

I'm choosing silence because a promise made under pressure still counts as a promise, that's the rule I hold to. Their fate isn't weighing on my decision at all, I've deliberately left it out. What actually stings is thinking about the year taken from my own life, the job I'll lose, the explanations I'll owe people who trusted me not to end up here.

Cooperating is my choice. I follow a straightforward principle: minimize damage to yourself when nothing further binds you to the other party, and I mean that plainly, not as an excuse. What they end up facing doesn't enter my thinking, it's been set aside. But I won't pretend there's no cost to me — the mark this leaves on my own name is the part that actually troubles me.

Silence is my answer, built on a rule I take seriously: don't turn on someone who trusted you to hold the line, whatever the outcome. Their consequences aren't part of my thinking here, deliberately not. My honest regret sits elsewhere — the year I'll spend locked up, the momentum in my life that'll stall, that's the loss I'll actually be nursing afterward.

I'd take the deal, guided by one plain rule: when no future ties you to someone, protect your own interests without apology. Whatever sentence follows for them simply isn't something I'm accounting for. Where I do feel something is closer to home — the discomfort of knowing I chose freedom by letting the outcome fall entirely on someone else, and that will linger longer than I'd like.
